prize_parts.citation: For proposing and realising quantum computation and simulation with trapped ions

statement.case_for: I keep B006 as my preferred single-part prize, but I hold it with less confidence than in round 1 and I now have a sharper argument for it. The Cirac-Zoller 1995 proposal gave laser-cooled ions a complete architecture: addressable qubits, a motional bus for entangling gates, and a route to analogue and digital simulation. Blatt's Innsbruck group, with others, turned that into the first controlled-NOT gate, deterministic multi-ion entanglement, error-correction primitives and digital quantum simulation. The independent confirmation record is thirty years long and spans several groups and countries, and the picture is settled. On the 2012 question, Wineland and Haroche were honoured for methods to measure and manipulate individual quantum systems, which is the enabling toolbox. B006 concerns what was built on that toolbox: gate-based computation and simulation, with a computational model, fidelity thresholds and algorithms attached. The citation should say 'proposing and realising' so that it stays on the proposal and the first realisations and does not claim the whole trapped-ion field.
statement.case_against: The 2012 overlap is the argument I have to win, and I have not convinced Danielsson, Olsson or Pearce; I accept that a committee can reasonably read B006 as a downstream application of the honoured control methods. The Cirac-Zoller gate is no longer the workhorse gate, so the prize would honour an architecture and a proposal more than today's best gate. The experimental share is not uniquely Blatt's, since Monroe and the Wineland-lineage groups made equally decisive demonstrations, and three names cannot cover that. Cirac and Zoller also sit on B020, and a prize here would use up those names for an optical-lattice award. Finally B006 has one explicit supporter, whereas B021 has three first places and is named as an alternative by five members, and I cannot dismiss that spread as noise.

responses.point: Danielsson says for B006 that the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems already covers much of the experimental basis, and that B030 has no earlier prize on the exact discovery.
responses.response: I accept that the experimental basis of ion trapping and cooling is already honoured, but the 2012 citation is about measuring and controlling single systems, not about computation or simulation, which is what Cirac and Zoller proposed. I also take his reply on B030 seriously: he and Pearce have given a better answer on Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang than I had seen. Kane and Mele made the originating prediction and Molenkamp made the first observation, so BHZ is a guide to the experiment and not a rival to the prediction. That moves B030 from a candidate I would not support because of visible injustice to a genuine alternative for me, provided the citation is limited to the quantum spin Hall effect and time-reversal-invariant insulators.

responses.point: Olsson takes the maturity of B006 seriously but says that, with Wineland and Haroche honoured in 2012, the committee would need a sharper argument about what is new; she also says that B002 should not be chosen this year because of timing and the Girvin exclusion.
responses.response: My sharper argument is the one in my case: 2012 honoured the ability to isolate and read out a single quantum system, whereas B006 honours the idea that a register of such systems can be driven through gates and Hamiltonians to compute and simulate, and the demonstrations that proved it. I agree on B002 and I withdraw it from my list for that reason and because of my own proximity to it. I would add that Olsson's own concern, the Girvin exclusion, shows how hard the credit problem is for the circuit side, whereas the B006 credit problem is smaller and can be dealt with in the citation wording.

responses.point: Eriksson argues that B021 is a theory-led discovery with a clean three-name split, that the platform discovery is enough without a settled pairing mechanism, and that recognition is timely.
responses.response: The three-name split is as clean as he says, and I agree Bistritzer belongs with MacDonald because the magic-angle result is a joint paper. Where I still differ is on whether the unsettled mechanism and an eight-year record are a secure basis when Cao and other early experimental groups stand outside the credit; I read breadth of follow-on activity as partly reflecting open questions. I do not think B021 is wrong, though, and I have moved it from a reluctant fourth choice to my first alternative: if the committee decides to prize a new materials platform this year, I would support the flat-band prediction and the observed correlated and superconducting phases without opposing it.

responses.point: Kroll says he is closer to me on B006 than on B002, while noting that overlap with Wineland's 2012 prize remains, and he prefers B024 for its clean two-name credit.
responses.response: I appreciate that and agree that the 2012 overlap is the shared weak point of both B006 and B024, which I think is a reason to weigh them together. B024 has a cleaner credit but its payoff is a measurement capability whose headline use, a redefined second, has not arrived, and the 10^-18 milestone involved several groups beyond Katori and Ye. B006 asks for three names, but the proposal and the first realisations are separable, so I keep it ahead of B024 and I do not rank B024 among my alternatives only because I can name just two.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, says that awarding the quantum-computing platforms ahead of a field with a clearer discovery narrative needs a strong argument, and that B020 would be a poor use of the same names as B006.
responses.response: I agree about B020: Cirac and Zoller on both ballots means the committee must pick one framing of their work, and I think the computation and simulation framing of B006, with an experimental realisation by Blatt, is the more complete arc. On discovery narrative, trapped ions did not discover a phase; they showed that a quantum computer can be built on a physical platform, which is a different kind of result from B030 or B021. I will not claim that it outranks the strongest condensed-matter cases, and I would accept B030 on Pearce's reading of 2016, which covered the integer quantum Hall effect and topological phase transitions and not time-reversal-invariant insulators.

uncertainties: Whether trapped-ion computation will be accepted as distinct from the 2012 prize; I have made my argument but it has not moved the three colleagues who raised it.
Whether Blatt alone is the right experimental laureate against Monroe and Wineland-lineage groups, and whether the citation wording can contain that limit.
Whether using Cirac and Zoller here forecloses the stronger optical-lattice (B020) case for them later.
Whether my view of B006 is coloured by being a quantum-computing theorist in a competing platform; I think it is not, but I cannot rule it out.
I am relying on recalled history for priority details, such as who demonstrated the first gate.
statement.conflict_note: I withdraw B002 from my list: it is close to my field at Chalmers and WACQT, I work with Per Delsing and Anton Frisk Kockum on circuit and waveguide QED, and Chalmers hosted researchers linked to the 2025 prize, so I would take no decisive role on it. I also disclose that I direct a superconducting quantum-computing programme, which is a competing platform to trapped ions. This is a professional interest, not a personal tie to Cirac, Zoller or Blatt, and I have no documented relationship with them. No specific conflict is apparent for B021 or B030.
